forbearance

/for-BAIR-uhns/ - the stress falls on BAIR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Forbearance means patience and self-restraint when provoked.

Mrs. Idowu bore the trumpet practice next door with a forbearance that never once curdled into a complaint.

Example

For eleven years the bookshop's loudest regular has mispronounced every author he buys, brought paperbacks back half-read with the spines cracked, and lectured the owner on stocking 'real literature.' She bears it all with forbearance: she trades the damaged copies out, recommends his next book, and has never once told him what she thinks of his manners.

Forbearance is the exact word for the owner's restraint, because forbearance means patience and self-restraint when provoked — and the provocation is standing at her register, weekly. Patience alone is tested by delay; forbearance is tested by insult, and it holds anyway.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

restraint: Restraint is holding yourself back from any impulse at all — spending, bragging, the second dessert. Forbearance is restraint of one particular kind: you have been provoked, the sharp reply is ready and deserved, and you hold it back and stay kind anyway.

tolerance: Tolerance is putting up with what you dislike — noise, habits, opinions — often by simply deciding it is not your business. Forbearance is more personal and harder won: the provocation is aimed at you, it stings, and you still choose not to answer the sting in kind.

composure: Composure is the steady surface — the level voice and unshaken face a person keeps under stress, with no promise about what happens next. Forbearance goes past appearances: provoked and stung, you not only stay steady but choose not to answer the insult at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

irritability: flaring at the smallest annoyance

vengefulness: answering every offense in kind

Where it sits · how much provocation it calmly absorbs

politeness → patience → forbearance

politeness vs. forbearance: Politeness is the mildest rung, well below forbearance — you can be perfectly polite to a customer who has done nothing to try you, while forbearance only begins once real provocation lands.

patience vs. forbearance: Patience goes further than politeness — it stays calm through long delays — but patience is tested by time, while forbearance is tested by insult.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — for-: against, holding off (Old English)

Root — bear: to carry, to endure

Suffix — -ance: noun ending: the act of

Put it together: For- (holding off) + bear (to carry, endure) + -ance = the act of bearing it while holding off. The old verb forbear meant to refrain — to carry the weight of an offense without setting it down on the offender — and forbearance is that carrying, made into a noun.

Use the root in a new word: unbearable: By August the attic apartment was unbearable, and she dragged her mattress out to the porch.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / admiring

Forbearance is the grown-up of the patience family: it holds steady while being provoked, and it chooses not to answer in kind. Its unit-mates work nearby — lenient softens the punishment an authority hands down, tactful takes the wounding words out of a sentence, accommodating rearranges plans. Forbearance simply absorbs the sting and stays kind.
